title: Buying Pellmoor
briefing: Valtren wants to buy Pellmoor Freight, a regional refrigerated haulier with pharma customers, for 9.5 million. The deal team is excited; the board wants the risk view before signing.
As Senior Risk Manager you lead the risk due diligence.

context.text: Hollis reminds the deal team that the stress-test triggers you agreed still apply: the acquisition must not push cash below the covenant in the combined scenario.
Your standard register method makes it easy to compare Pellmoor's risks with Valtren's.

evidence.title: Pellmoor financials
evidence.body: Revenue 14m, margin 9% (Valtren: 7%). 41% of revenue from one pharma client whose contract renews in 7 months.

evidence.title: Due diligence findings
body: Fleet: average age 9 years (Valtren: 5). Two vehicles failed temperature mapping last year.
Compliance: Good Distribution Practice licence renewed with 'minor findings'; corrective actions not closed.
People: the founder runs all client relationships and will leave 6 months after completion.

evidence.title: Proposed terms
evidence.body: 9.5m at completion, funded mostly by a new bank loan with 1.5m from Valtren's cash. No earn-out. Standard warranties capped at 10% of price.

questions.prompt: Which risks should most shape the deal?

options.label: 41% of revenue from one client renewing in 7 months
The founder holds every client relationship and leaves in 6 months
Old fleet with failed temperature mapping and open GDP findings, in exactly the pharma work Valtren is buying
Pellmoor's higher margin
options.feedback: A reason to buy, not a risk to manage, though it may not survive the client renewal.

questions.prompt: What do you recommend to the board? (Your authority is 750,000; this decision is the board's.)

options.label: Proceed only with protections: part of the price as an earn-out tied to the pharma client renewing, a founder transition agreement, fleet and GDP fixes priced into the deal, and higher warranty caps
options.feedback: Keeps the strategic prize and moves the identified risks back to the seller.

options.label: Sign as proposed; the strategic fit is too good to lose
options.feedback: The board pays full price for risks you identified.

schedules.description: Pellmoor's largest pharma client does not renew after the founder leaves

options.label: Walk away
options.feedback: Safe, but abandons a strategic route into pharma that protections could have secured.

questions.prompt: If the pharma client (41% of 14m revenue) leaves and Pellmoor's 9% margin applies, roughly how much annual margin is at risk?
The deal team says your findings will 'kill the deal'. How do you work with them?

options.label: Show them each risk with a deal protection that addresses it, so the findings strengthen the negotiating position
options.feedback: Turns risk findings into negotiating leverage.

options.label: Bypass them and brief the board alone
options.feedback: The board will hear two stories and trust neither.

options.label: Soften the findings to keep relationships good
options.feedback: Your independence is the reason the board asked.

questions.prompt: After signing, what is the first risk action for integration?

options.label: A named relationship lead shadowing the founder from day one, with a renewal plan for the pharma client
options.feedback: Addresses the risk with the shortest fuse.

options.label: Rebrand the trucks
options.feedback: Visible but irrelevant to the main risks.

options.label: Migrate Pellmoor to Valtren's IT systems
options.feedback: Needed later; the client renewal comes first.

lesson: In a deal, risk work earns its keep by changing the terms: price, earn-outs and warranties can move identified risks back to the seller.
